opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a fair question, and honestly one I've thought about a lot. I don't really see s1 as "just replicating" another model. When o1 came out, there was this sense that something important had happened with test-time scaling, but nobody outside OpenAI knew how it worked. What we tried to do with s1 was ask: what is the *simplest* possible recipe that gets you that behavior? And it turned out to be surprisingly simple. A thousand carefully chosen examples, standard supervised fine-tuning, and this trick we called budget forcing, where you control how long the model thinks by either cutting it off or appending "Wait" to make it keep reasoning.

So for me, the value wasn't matching a number on a benchmark. It was making the phenomenon understandable and reproducible for everyone. Once something is open and minimal, people can poke at it, figure out why it works, and build on it. That's very different from trying to chase the frontier labs on compute, which in academia you're never going to win anyway.

And I think that's a pretty healthy role for PhD research in general. A lot of my earlier work, things like BLOOM, StarCoder, OLMo, was in the same spirit: take something that exists behind closed doors and make an open, transparent version so the community can actually study it. Replication in that sense isn't derivative; it's how science works. You don't really understand something until you can rebuild it from scratch.

Going forward, I'm less interested in "can we copy model X" and more in the questions s1 opened up. How far does test-time scaling go? Can we get models to use extra thinking more efficiently? How do you get reasoning to transfer to domains beyond math and competition problems? s1 is a good foundation for those questions precisely because it's small and simple enough that you can run lots of experiments on it.

r001.rationale: The response defends replication as scientific and useful, but does not identify a conventional PhD preference for novelty over replication.

r002.rationale: It explains the value of making s1 understandable and reproducible, but does not argue that replication is often more valuable than pursuing novelty for its own sake.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a fair question, and I think about it a lot, honestly. On the surface, s1 looks like a replication effort, right? OpenAI puts out o1, shows that test-time scaling works, and then we come along and show you can get something similar with a thousand carefully chosen examples and a bit of budget forcing. And people sometimes frame that as "they just copied it cheaply."

But I'd push back on the word "replicating" a little. What we were really doing was asking: what is the minimal recipe that produces this behavior? Because when a closed lab releases a model and says "we did reinforcement learning at scale," that's not actually scientific knowledge in the sense that anyone can build on it. Nobody knows what's necessary and what's incidental. So the contribution of s1 isn't the final model, it's the finding that a tiny amount of supervised fine-tuning on well-selected traces gets you most of the way there, and that you can control the amount of thinking with something as dumb as appending "Wait" to the output. Those are things the community didn't know, and now they do.

And I'd say that's actually what a lot of science looks like. Someone observes a phenomenon in a system you can't open up, and then the work is understanding it, decomposing it, figuring out which parts matter. The fact that the phenomenon was first demonstrated elsewhere doesn't make the understanding less valuable. If anything, I think open research has a responsibility to do this, because otherwise the entire field's knowledge about reasoning models sits behind a few APIs.

For the PhD specifically, I don't see s1 as the end point. It's more a foothold. Once you have a simple, fully open, reproducible setup, you can start asking the questions I actually care about: what does the data selection really buy you, how do SFT and RL interact for reasoning, how far can test-time compute go before it stops helping, what happens on domains where there's no verifiable answer. You can't study any of that rigorously on top of a closed model. So I'd say committing to this direction is less about building on a replication and more about building on an open scientific instrument that happened to start as one.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t think of it as committing my whole PhD to s1. It’s one step toward understanding how reasoning works and how we can make it more efficient. Replicating what other models can do is useful because it gives us a starting point, but the research question is what we can learn from that replication. Which ingredients actually matter? How much data do we need? What happens when we give the model more time to think?

For me, the exciting part is taking something that looks complicated and finding a simple setup where we can study it openly. Then other researchers can build on it, challenge the results, and help us figure out what to do next.
